title: When to Call a Handyman vs. a General Contractor
seoTitle: Handyman vs. General Contractor: When to Call Which
seoDescription: Not every project needs a full contractor crew. Learn what a handyman does well, when a general contractor is needed and the middle ground.
html:
One of the most common questions homeowners ask is whether their project needs a licensed general contractor or whether a skilled handyman is the right call. The answer comes down to scale, permits, and trade involvement. For a list of the repairs that almost always fall in handyman territory, see 5 Small Home Repairs You Shouldn't Put Off.

What a Handyman Does Well

A handyman excels at a broad range of smaller, defined tasks: fixing drywall, replacing fixtures, caulking, painting, minor carpentry, TV mounting, ceiling fan installation, deck repairs, and general maintenance. These are discrete jobs with clear scope — the kind that would cost a homeowner hours of learning on YouTube but take a skilled handyman an hour or two.

The economic advantage of a handyman is significant on these tasks. You're not paying for the overhead of a contracting company, a project manager, or subcontractor coordination. You get focused labour on the specific job at hand.

When You Need a General Contractor

General contractors are the right choice when a project requires permits, involves multiple trades, or has significant structural components. A kitchen gut renovation, an addition, a basement that requires electrical panel upgrades and new plumbing rough-in — these involve coordination between electricians, plumbers, framers, and inspectors that falls squarely in a GC's wheelhouse.

If your project requires a building permit, start there. A permit tells you upfront whether you're in GC territory. In Ontario, work like structural alterations, new electrical circuits, plumbing modifications, and HVAC changes all typically require permits and licensed tradespeople.

The Middle Ground

Many projects live between these two poles. A bathroom refresh — new vanity, toilet, shower fixtures, tile work, and a fresh coat of paint — often doesn't require permits or a GC, but it's more involved than a single handyman task. An experienced handyman with broad skills can often handle exactly this type of multi-task project efficiently.

When in doubt, describe your project in detail and ask. A reliable handyman will tell you honestly if the job is outside their scope. That kind of straightforwardness is actually a good sign you've found someone worth working with.
